2026-03-13.teaser: Today's collection spans the full spectrum of technological disruption and its real-world consequences. We've got breakthrough energy plays that could reshape manufacturing, shocking security breaches that expose the vulnerability of enterprise AI systems, and deep dives into how entire industries operate in regulatory gray zones. From Chinese AI companies building on open-source foundations to the shadowy economics of online gaming, these stories reveal the messy, complex reality behind the headlines. Each piece offers something you won't find in your typical tech coverage.

included.title: How We Hacked McKinsey's AI Platform
included.source: X/Twitter bookmark via Dr Efi Pylarinou
included.summary: A security research team at CodeWall.AI successfully breached McKinsey's enterprise AI platform, Lilly, using autonomous agents to access massive amounts of sensitive data without authentication. The hack exposed 46.5 million chat messages and revealed fundamental security vulnerabilities in enterprise AI systems that are increasingly trusted with confidential business information. The breach highlights a critical gap between the rapid deployment of AI platforms and the implementation of robust security measures. The autonomous nature of the attack demonstrates how AI tools can be weaponized against AI systems, creating new categories of cyber threats. The scale of accessible data suggests that many organizations may be unknowingly exposing sensitive information through poorly secured AI interfaces. This incident raises urgent questions about data governance, authentication protocols, and the security architecture of enterprise AI platforms that handle confidential business communications and strategic information.

included.title: The Shadow Economy of Online Gaming: How Money Moves Beyond the Screen
included.summary: An investigative report reveals how banks, payment processors, and aggregators collaborated to enable transactions for shadow gaming operators by disguising them as legitimate e-commerce merchants. The investigation exposes a sophisticated network where gaming companies that couldn't secure direct payment processing relationships were quietly onboarded through alternative channels, circumventing regulatory oversight and compliance requirements. This shadow payment ecosystem allowed potentially illegal or unregulated gaming operations to process billions in transactions while appearing as standard retail businesses to financial institutions. The report details how payment aggregators served as intermediaries, creating layers of obfuscation that made it difficult for banks to identify the true nature of the underlying businesses. The investigation raises serious questions about due diligence practices in the payments industry and the effectiveness of current regulatory frameworks in monitoring high-risk sectors. The findings have implications for anti-money laundering compliance, consumer protection, and the broader integrity of digital payment systems that increasingly power the global economy.

included.title: OpenClaw: China's AI Stack
included.summary: Zhipu's launch of AutoClaw represents the culmination of a remarkable trend where every major Chinese AI company has built products around a single open-source project, creating an ecosystem that includes Moonshot's KimiClaw, MiniMax's MaxClaw, Alibaba's CoPaw, ByteDance's ArkClaw, and Tencent's WorkBuddy. This convergence around one foundational technology demonstrates how open-source projects can become the backbone of an entire national AI strategy, creating both opportunities and dependencies. The market response was immediate, with Zhipu's stock jumping 13% on the announcement, indicating investor confidence in this approach to AI development. This phenomenon highlights the power of open-source in democratizing AI capabilities while raising questions about technological sovereignty and the concentration of innovation around specific platforms. The Chinese AI companies' collective embrace of this technology stack suggests a coordinated approach to building competitive AI products without reinventing fundamental infrastructure. This strategy could accelerate innovation by allowing companies to focus on application-layer differentiation while sharing underlying technological foundations, though it also creates potential single points of failure for the entire ecosystem.

included.title: Swift Solar Acquires Meyer Burger to Build Gigawatt-Scale Solar Factory
included.summary: Swift Solar's acquisition of Meyer Burger represents a strategic shift from component supplier to end-product manufacturer, embodying the principle that superior technology should be used to compete directly rather than simply sold to others. Joel Jean at Swift Solar is applying this philosophy to solar manufacturing, using their advanced perovskite tandem solar cell technology to build a gigawatt-scale factory capable of producing highly efficient solar panels. The deal gives Swift Solar access to Meyer Burger's established manufacturing infrastructure and expertise, allowing them to scale their innovative technology rapidly. This vertical integration strategy challenges the traditional model where technology companies license their innovations to manufacturers, instead betting that controlling the entire value chain will create sustainable competitive advantages. The gigawatt-scale ambition signals Swift Solar's intention to compete directly with established solar panel manufacturers while leveraging their technological edge in efficiency. This approach could accelerate the adoption of next-generation solar technology by removing the intermediary step of technology licensing and ensuring that the most advanced innovations reach the market quickly. The acquisition demonstrates how breakthrough energy technologies are increasingly being paired with aggressive scaling strategies.

included.title: ITR Forms AY 2025-26: More Disclosures, Details on HRA, Home Loan, TDS
included.summary: India's new ITR forms for Assessment Year 2025-26 introduce significant changes that expand disclosure requirements and modify filing procedures for taxpayers. The most substantial change raises the asset disclosure threshold from ₹50 lakh to ₹1 crore in income, requiring high earners to provide comprehensive details of all assets in Schedule AL. This change affects a smaller but wealthier segment of taxpayers while reducing compliance burden for middle-income earners. The forms now allow taxpayers with long-term capital gains below ₹1.25 lakh to use simplified ITR-1 or ITR-4 forms, streamlining the filing process for small investors. Enhanced requirements for HRA and deduction details provide tax authorities with more granular information about common tax-saving claims, potentially improving compliance monitoring. A crucial addition requires separate reporting of capital gains before and after July 23, 2024, corresponding to budget changes that likely affected tax rates or exemptions. These modifications reflect the tax authority's dual approach of simplifying procedures for smaller taxpayers while increasing scrutiny and disclosure requirements for high-income individuals. The changes demonstrate India's evolving tax administration strategy, balancing ease of compliance with improved revenue collection and taxpayer monitoring.

included.title: Sarvam: Open is not sovereign
included.summary: This analysis challenges the conventional wisdom that open-source AI models automatically confer technological sovereignty, using Sarvam as a case study to examine the complex relationship between openness and independence in AI development. The piece argues that while open-source models provide access to code and weights, true sovereignty requires control over the entire AI value chain, including data, compute infrastructure, talent, and the ability to modify and improve foundational models independently. The author contends that countries and companies relying heavily on open-source models from foreign entities may actually be increasing their technological dependence rather than achieving independence. The analysis explores how Sarvam's approach to building AI capabilities intersects with broader questions about national AI strategies and the trade-offs between leveraging global open-source resources and developing indigenous capabilities. The piece examines whether open-source AI creates a false sense of technological autonomy while potentially deepening dependencies on the ecosystems, tools, and platforms controlled by the original model creators. This perspective challenges policymakers and technologists to think more critically about what genuine AI sovereignty requires in an increasingly interconnected global technology landscape.

2026-03-14.teaser: Today's picks dive deep into two critical shifts reshaping global finance and technology. We explore the brewing storm in private credit markets, where warning signs from major fund managers suggest defaults could double in coming years. Meanwhile, we examine the complex relationship between open-source AI development and national sovereignty, questioning whether 'open' truly means independent. These stories reveal the hidden tensions between innovation, regulation, and control that define our economic moment.

included.title: What's going on with private credit?
included.summary: Private credit markets are showing serious stress signals, with industry leaders warning of potential crisis ahead. Steffen Meister from Partners Group, managing over $180 billion, predicts default rates could double in coming years. The article explains how private credit emerged as banks retreated from lending after 2008 financial regulations, creating space for non-bank lenders to fill the gap. These private credit funds offer loans to mid-market companies that can't access public bond markets, typically charging higher rates than traditional banks. The current concern stems from several factors: funds are freezing withdrawals, marking down asset values, and some portfolio companies are failing. Unlike traditional banking with deposit insurance and regulatory oversight, private credit operates with less transparency and protection. The warning signs include overleveraged borrowers, aggressive lending standards during the low-rate environment, and potential liquidity mismatches as economic conditions tighten. This situation echoes pre-2008 dynamics where alternative lending grew rapidly with insufficient risk assessment. The article contextualizes this for Indian readers, noting private credit's relative novelty in India compared to its $1.7 trillion size in the US market.

2026-03-15.teaser: The global economy's most vulnerable chokepoint is making headlines again, while India's fintech sector faces a wave of regulatory changes and strategic pivots. From oil tankers stuck outside the Strait of Hormuz to AI agents revolutionizing business workflows, this week's picks reveal how narrow passages—whether geographic or technological—can reshape entire industries. Meanwhile, the intersection of artificial intelligence and payments is creating new possibilities for commerce, even as traditional players scramble to adapt to an increasingly digital-first world.

included.title: The chokepoint that powers the global economy
included.summary: The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow 33-kilometer waterway between Iran and Oman, has become the focal point of global energy security concerns following recent military conflicts in the region. This seemingly insignificant geographic feature carries enormous economic weight—approximately 20 million barrels of oil and a fifth of global LNG supply pass through it daily. When US-Israeli strikes on Iran triggered retaliatory actions across the Gulf, the strait's vulnerability became starkly apparent as ships stopped moving and insurers pulled back coverage. Goldman Sachs data reveals that 13.4 million barrels per day of crude exports moved through this route in 2025, primarily from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, and the UAE. While alternative pipeline routes exist, they can only handle about 4.2 million barrels per day according to the International Energy Agency. The disruption created a logistics nightmare, with over 200 oil and LNG vessels anchored outside the strait as shipowners refused to risk transit through an active conflict zone. This bottleneck effect demonstrates how modern global commerce remains dependent on a handful of critical geographic passages, where even temporary disruptions can cascade into worldwide economic impacts.

included.title: Starting AI Today? This Is Exactly What I'd Do
included.summary: A 54-year-old political consultant's transformation from AI skeptic to power user illustrates a fundamental shift in how professionals should approach artificial intelligence. Rather than viewing AI as a replacement threat, the author argues it should be seen as a force multiplier that amplifies existing expertise and experience. The consultant, initially fearing obsolescence, learned to combine his 20 years of industry knowledge with AI's speed and execution capabilities, ultimately building six AI agents that could produce a $75,000 consulting proposal in three hours. The key insight is moving beyond treating AI like a search engine—asking questions and copying answers—to giving AI the ability to act directly within your work environment. This means using tools like code editors (Cursor, VS Code + Claude) that allow AI to see files, create content, and fix its own mistakes autonomously. The author emphasizes that learning to code isn't necessary; rather, the focus should be on developing a new way of thinking about AI as an active collaborator rather than a passive tool. This mindset shift, combined with giving AI 'hands' to work in your digital environment, represents the difference between basic AI usage and truly transformative productivity gains.

included.title: Perplexity Computer vs Claude: Pick the Right AI Agent
included.summary: Perplexity Computer represents a new category of AI tool that functions as a 'project machine' rather than a traditional chatbot, dynamically routing tasks across 19 frontier models including Claude Opus 4.6, Google Gemini, and GPT-5.2. Unlike single-model approaches, Perplexity's architecture leverages each model's strengths—Claude for coding, Gemini for research, GPT-5.2 for long-context tasks—while orchestrating complex workflows that can build market dashboards or research presentations from single prompts. At $200/month for 10,000 credits (with heavy users reporting actual costs of $500-1,500), it targets users coordinating real workflows across Gmail, Slack, Notion, and GitHub rather than simple question-answering. The comparison with Claude's suite (Desktop, Code, and Cowork) reveals different philosophies: Perplexity bets on the aggregator layer being the winning position, while Claude focuses on deep integration within specific environments. The key differentiator lies in use case—if you're answering questions, cheaper tools suffice, but if you're orchestrating multi-step projects across various platforms, Perplexity Computer's ability to break jobs into smaller tasks, spin up specialized helpers, and deliver finished outputs justifies its premium pricing. The 19-model architecture represents a significant technical advancement in AI orchestration.

included.title: CBI searches 15 locations to investigate cyber fraud network
included.summary: The Central Bureau of Investigation has uncovered a sophisticated transnational cybercrime network that allegedly defrauded victims of approximately Rs 900 crore through fake online investment and part-time job schemes. The operation, led by chartered accountant Ashok Kumar Sharma, used social media platforms and encrypted messaging to lure victims with promises of high returns, initially allowing small deposits and showing fictitious profits to build trust before encouraging larger investments. The fraud's sophistication lay in its money laundering mechanism—funds were rapidly moved through multiple mule bank accounts before being withdrawn at offshore ATMs or converted through Dubai-based fintech platform Pyypl. In a parallel operation, Sharma allegedly used 15 shell companies to convert Rs 900 crore into Tether stablecoins (USDT) via Indian virtual asset exchanges, then transferred the cryptocurrency to whitelisted wallets. The CBI's coordinated searches across Delhi, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, and Punjab revealed that several shell company directors were unsuspecting individuals fraudulently appointed using forged documentation. This case highlights the growing threat of cross-border financial crimes that exploit both traditional banking systems and emerging fintech platforms, demonstrating how criminals are adapting to use legitimate financial infrastructure for illicit purposes while leveraging cryptocurrency for final fund extraction.

included.title: Neobank Fi closes banking services on its platform
included.summary: Fi, the neobank startup backed by Peak XV Partners and other prominent investors, has shut down its digital banking services and redirected users to partner Federal Bank's channels, marking a significant strategic pivot away from consumer-first digital banking. Founded in 2019 by Sujith Narayan and Sumit Gwalani with the mission of making banking 'more thoughtful and human,' Fi had raised $169 million and built a user base of primarily young Indians through simplified onboarding, gamification features, and financial literacy programs. The closure represents more than just a product shutdown—it signals a broader industry reckoning with the neobanking model in India. Cofounder Narayan indicated in February that the company would realign toward 'deep technology, AI, and building complex systems for startups & large enterprises,' suggesting Fi recognized that sustainable differentiation lay in B2B infrastructure rather than consumer-facing banking products. This pivot reflects the challenges many neobanks face in achieving profitability while competing with established banks that have regulatory advantages and deeper pockets. Fi's decision to exit consumer banking while maintaining its partnership with Federal Bank demonstrates how fintech companies are increasingly focusing on their core technological strengths rather than trying to replicate traditional banking services.

included.title: PayU partners with CoRover.ai to enable AI-led agentic payments
included.summary: PayU's strategic partnership with CoRover.ai represents a pioneering effort to integrate conversational AI with payment infrastructure, potentially transforming how India's next 500 million users—who are primarily voice-first and conversational—interact with digital commerce. The collaboration integrates PayU's payment infrastructure with CoRover's BharatGPT-powered conversational Agentic AI platform, creating what the companies claim is one of the first partnerships between a sovereign Large Language Model provider and a payment aggregator. BharatGPT, CoRover's enterprise-grade LLM that attracted investment from HDFC Bank, enables AI-driven payments across multiple Indian languages and dialects, addressing a crucial accessibility barrier in digital payments. The concept of 'agentic payments' represents a fundamental shift from traditional transaction models—instead of users navigating through apps and forms, AI agents can understand intent, complete tasks, and execute payments securely within natural conversations. This approach could be particularly transformative in India, where language barriers and digital literacy challenges have limited fintech adoption among certain demographics. PayU's Chief Product Officer Manas Mishra's observation that 'the next phase of digital payments will happen inside AI-led conversations' suggests this partnership is positioning for a future where commerce becomes truly frictionless through conversational interfaces.

included.title: Cred gets RBI's final nod to operate as payment aggregator
included.summary: Cred's receipt of final RBI approval to operate as a payment aggregator marks another milestone in the Reserve Bank of India's systematic licensing of fintech players, while positioning Kunal Shah's company to expand beyond its credit card payment roots into broader merchant services. The authorization allows Cred to onboard merchants, process payments on their behalf, and manage settlements and refunds across payment instruments—capabilities that could significantly diversify its revenue streams beyond the rewards-based credit card model that made it famous. With this approval, Cred now holds multiple regulatory licenses across payments, lending, insurance, and investments, creating a comprehensive financial services ecosystem. The timing is notable given Cred's valuation challenges—the company raised $72 million in June 2025 at a $3.5 billion valuation, significantly lower than its 2022 peak of $6.4 billion. This regulatory approval provides Cred with new monetization opportunities in the merchant payments space, potentially helping justify its valuation through diversified revenue streams. The RBI's recent activity in granting payment aggregator licenses to major players like Razorpay, Pine Labs, and Paytm suggests a broader regulatory push to formalize and strengthen India's digital payments infrastructure, with Cred now positioned as another key player in this ecosystem.
